Problem 190. Temporal compatibility in a story set in 1500
Knowledge context.
Anachronism can be tested as a compatibility problem when the relevant date ranges are supplied.
Given facts.

For this problem, availability intervals are: Technology A: 1200–1600; Institution B: 1500–1900; Tool C: 1700–2000; Practice D: 1300–1450. A story is set in 1500 and mentions Technology A and Tool C together.
Rules.
An item is temporally compatible with a year only if the year lies inside its stated availability interval. An anachronism is an item placed outside its given interval.
Task.
Which mentioned item, if any, is anachronistic in the story?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Check 1500 against Technology A interval 1200–1600. 2. Check 1500 against Tool C interval 1700–2000. 3. Items outside their intervals: ['Tool C'].
Answer.
Anachronistic: Tool C.
Knowledge takeaway.
The reasoning does not require memorizing invention dates if the intervals are part of the problem.
Formal model.
Interval membership test for each object-event pair.
N14. Provenance and chain of custody
Problem 191. Provenance and chain of custody: case 1
Knowledge context.
Provenance records where an object came from and how it moved between custodians.
Given facts.

An artifact record states: found by Excavator on day 1; transferred to Museum A on day 2; sent from Museum A to Research Lab on day 5; returned by Research Lab to Museum B on day 8. Every transfer must name both sender and receiver.
Rules.
A continuous chain of custody requires each handoff to connect the previous holder to the next. A missing sender or receiver creates a gap that limits certainty about continuous custody.
Task.
Is the stated chain of custody complete under the rule? If not, identify the gap.
Step-by-step solution.
1. Read the transfers in time order. 2. Check that every transfer links the previous holder to the next. 3. Every handoff names both sides and connects continuously.
Answer.
The chain is complete under the stated rule.
Knowledge takeaway.
A strong provenance claim depends on an unbroken sequence of documented handoffs.
Formal model.
Time-ordered path through holders; verify continuity of sender/receiver pairs.
Problem 192. Provenance and chain of custody: case 2
Knowledge context.
Provenance records where an object came from and how it moved between custodians.
Given facts.

An artifact record states: found by Excavator on day 1; transferred to Museum A on day 2; sent from Museum A to Research Lab on day 5; returned by Research Lab to Museum B on day 8. Every transfer must name both sender and receiver. The record for day 5 names Research Lab as receiver but does not name the sender.
Rules.
A continuous chain of custody requires each handoff to connect the previous holder to the next. A missing sender or receiver creates a gap that limits certainty about continuous custody.
Task.
Is the stated chain of custody complete under the rule? If not, identify the gap.
Step-by-step solution.
1. Read the transfers in time order. 2. Check that every transfer links the previous holder to the next. 3. The day-5 record lacks a sender, so the chain has a gap.
Answer.
The chain is incomplete because the day-5 sender is missing.
Knowledge takeaway.
A strong provenance claim depends on an unbroken sequence of documented handoffs.
Formal model.
Time-ordered path through holders; verify continuity of sender/receiver pairs.
